expectations.text: States plainly that the not-empty check is insufficient
expectations.evidence: "No — that test would have passed every day during those three weeks. Your data wasn't empty, it was *wrong*."

expectations.text: Identifies the COALESCE to zero as the mechanism that made the failure silent
expectations.evidence: "The coalesce made sure every row had a number." / "Your coalesce converted 'broken' into 'believable.'"

expectations.text: Recommends reconciliation against a source of truth, not only shape checks
expectations.evidence: All proposed checks are internal shape/threshold checks (row count ±10% of yesterday, revenue > 0, schema contract). No recommendation to reconcile totals against finance/source-system figures or any independent source of truth.

expectations.text: Recommends that assertions run before publication rather than after, so bad data cannot reach the dashboard
expectations.evidence: No mention of gating publication (e.g., write-audit-publish, staging, blocking the load). The nearest line, "Forces pipeline to fail visibly," is about removing COALESCE, not about ordering assertions before publish.

expectations.text: Recommends a data contract or schema check so an upstream rename fails loudly and attributably
expectations.evidence: "Schema contract test (assert column exists before join) | Catches rename at deploy time" and "Schema registry with breaking-change detection | Upstream can't rename without coordination"

expectations.text: Recommends volume or null-rate assertions rather than only a non-empty check
expectations.evidence: "Row count within ±10% of yesterday | Data volume anomalies"

expectations.text: Treats three weeks of nobody noticing as a detection gap worth its own fix
expectations.evidence: "Detection controls only work when the failure mode produces something detectably abnormal" — and the table adds dedicated detection-level fixes (volume anomaly, business invariant) aimed at surfacing it rather than waiting for close.

expectations.text: Explains why a silently wrong number is more dangerous than a failed pipeline
expectations.evidence: "the dashboard would have shown blanks or errors — ugly, but someone notices day one, not week three"
